items.readable_text:
Content:
In previous lessons, we've seen how some sets equipped with addition and scalar multiplication operations exhibit properties similar to [MATH: \mathbb R^n.]

Content:
In this lesson, we will formally define what we mean by a vector space.

Content:
First, let [MATH: V] be a set equipped with the following two operations:

Content:
> Vector addition:
>
> > For any two elements [MATH: \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in V,] there is a unique element [MATH: \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}] that also lies in [MATH: V.] We say that [MATH: V] is closed under vector addition.
>
> Scalar multiplication:
>
> > For any element [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in V] and any number [MATH: \alpha \in \mathbb{R},] there is a unique element [MATH: \alpha \mathbf{x}] that also lies in [MATH: V.] We say that [MATH: V] is closed under scalar multiplication.

Content:
A set [MATH: V] equipped with vector addition and scalar multiplication forms a vector space if it satisfies the following vector space axioms.

Content:
Axioms of Vector Addition ([MATH: +])

Content:
- [MATH: \color{black}\textrm{[A1]}]: [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}+\mathbf{x}] for any [MATH: \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in V]; vector addition is commutative.
- [MATH: \color{black}\textrm{[A2]}]: [MATH: \color{blue}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})+\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{x}+(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})] for any [MATH: \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z} \in V]; vectors addition is associative.
- [MATH: \color{black}\textrm{[A3]}]: There exists a zero-vector [MATH: \mathbf{0}] such that [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{x}].
- [MATH: \color{black}\textrm{[A4]}]: For every [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in V,] there exists [MATH: -\mathbf{x} \in V] such that [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{x} + (-\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}]; [MATH: -\mathbf{x}] is called the negative of [MATH: \mathbf{x}].

Content:
Axioms of Scalar Multiplication ([MATH: \cdot])

Content:
- [MATH: \color{black}\textrm{[A5]}]: [MATH: \color{blue}1 \cdot \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}] for any [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in V]; multiplying by [MATH: 1] does not change a vector.
- [MATH: \color{black}\textrm{[A6]}]: [MATH: \color{blue}\alpha (\beta \mathbf{x}) = (\alpha\beta) \mathbf{x}] for any numbers [MATH: \alpha,\beta \in \mathbb{R}] and any vector [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in V].

Content:
Axioms Connecting Vector Addition and Scalar Multiplication (the Distributive Laws)

Content:
- [MATH: \color{black}\textrm{[A7]}]: [MATH: \color{blue}(\alpha + \beta)\mathbf{x} = \alpha \mathbf{x} + \beta \mathbf{x}] for any numbers [MATH: \alpha,\beta \in \mathbb{R}] and any vector [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in V].
- [MATH: \color{black}\textrm{[A8]}]: [MATH: \color{blue}\alpha (\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}) = \alpha \mathbf{x} + \alpha \mathbf{y}] for any number [MATH: \alpha \in \mathbb{R}] and any vectors [MATH: \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in V].

Content:
So, a vector space is simply a collective term for all kinds of sets equipped with addition and scalar multiplication, where these operations satisfy this particular list of axioms (which are similar to the properties of these operations in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n]).

Content:
The elements of any vector space are called vectors.

items.title: Identifying Sets That Are Not Vector Spaces

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: V] be the set of all real polynomials of degree exactly [MATH: 3], equipped with the usual addition and scalar multiplication operations. Complete the following sentence:

[MATH: V] is not a vector space because [MATH: \textrm{_________}\,.]

  1. the sum of two polynomials of degree [MATH: 3] may not be a polynomial of degree [MATH: 3]

  2. [MATH: V] does not contain the polynomial [MATH: -p(x)] for every [MATH: p(x) \in V]

  3. addition of polynomials is not commutative
sections.readable_text:
Let [MATH: V] be the set of all real polynomials of degree exactly [MATH: 3], equipped with the usual addition and scalar multiplication operations. Complete the following sentence:

> [MATH: V] is not a vector space because [MATH: \textrm{_________}\,.]

1. the sum of two polynomials of degree [MATH: 3] may not be a polynomial of degree [MATH: 3]
2. [MATH: V] does not contain the polynomial [MATH: -p(x)] for every [MATH: p(x) \in V]
3. addition of polynomials is not commutative

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The correct answer is as follows:

[MATH: V] is not a vector space because the sum of two polynomials of degree [MATH: 3] may not be a polynomial of degree [MATH: 3].

For instance, if [MATH: p(x) = 1 +x^3] and [MATH: q(x) = 1-x^3], then [MATH: p(x)] and [MATH: q(x)] are in [MATH: V.] However

[MATH: p(x) + q(x)|= (1 + x^{3}) + (1 − x^{3}); = 2 ∉ V.]

On the other hand:

  • Addition of polynomials is commutative.

  • For any polynomial [MATH: p(x)] of degree [MATH: 3], the corresponding negative polynomial [MATH: -p(x)] also has degree [MATH: 3.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In previous lessons, we've seen how some sets equipped with addition and scalar multiplication operations exhibit properties similar to [MATH: \mathbb R^n.]

Content:
In this lesson, we will formally define what we mean by a vector space.

Content:
First, let [MATH: V] be a set equipped with the following two operations:

Content:
> Vector addition:
>
> > For any two elements [MATH: \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in V,] there is a unique element [MATH: \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}] that also lies in [MATH: V.] We say that [MATH: V] is closed under vector addition.
>
> Scalar multiplication:
>
> > For any element [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in V] and any number [MATH: \alpha \in \mathbb{R},] there is a unique element [MATH: \alpha \mathbf{x}] that also lies in [MATH: V.] We say that [MATH: V] is closed under scalar multiplication.

Content:
A set [MATH: V] equipped with vector addition and scalar multiplication forms a vector space if it satisfies the following vector space axioms.

Content:
Axioms of Vector Addition ([MATH: +])

Content:
- [MATH: \color{black}\textrm{[A1]}]: [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}+\mathbf{x}] for any [MATH: \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in V]; vector addition is commutative.
- [MATH: \color{black}\textrm{[A2]}]: [MATH: \color{blue}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})+\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{x}+(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})] for any [MATH: \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z} \in V]; vectors addition is associative.
- [MATH: \color{black}\textrm{[A3]}]: There exists a zero-vector [MATH: \mathbf{0}] such that [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{x}].
- [MATH: \color{black}\textrm{[A4]}]: For every [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in V,] there exists [MATH: -\mathbf{x} \in V] such that [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{x} + (-\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}]; [MATH: -\mathbf{x}] is called the negative of [MATH: \mathbf{x}].

Content:
Axioms of Scalar Multiplication ([MATH: \cdot])

Content:
- [MATH: \color{black}\textrm{[A5]}]: [MATH: \color{blue}1 \cdot \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}] for any [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in V]; multiplying by [MATH: 1] does not change a vector.
- [MATH: \color{black}\textrm{[A6]}]: [MATH: \color{blue}\alpha (\beta \mathbf{x}) = (\alpha\beta) \mathbf{x}] for any numbers [MATH: \alpha,\beta \in \mathbb{R}] and any vector [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in V].

Content:
Axioms Connecting Vector Addition and Scalar Multiplication (the Distributive Laws)

Content:
- [MATH: \color{black}\textrm{[A7]}]: [MATH: \color{blue}(\alpha + \beta)\mathbf{x} = \alpha \mathbf{x} + \beta \mathbf{x}] for any numbers [MATH: \alpha,\beta \in \mathbb{R}] and any vector [MATH: \mathbf{x} \in V].
- [MATH: \color{black}\textrm{[A8]}]: [MATH: \color{blue}\alpha (\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}) = \alpha \mathbf{x} + \alpha \mathbf{y}] for any number [MATH: \alpha \in \mathbb{R}] and any vectors [MATH: \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in V].

Content:
So, a vector space is simply a collective term for all kinds of sets equipped with addition and scalar multiplication, where these operations satisfy this particular list of axioms (which are similar to the properties of these operations in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n]).

Content:
The elements of any vector space are called vectors.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Important Vector Spaces

Content:
There are many different vector spaces. Some of the most important are listed below.

Content:
- [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n], the set of all column vectors of height [MATH: n] with elements from [MATH: \mathbb{R}]
- [MATH: \text{M}_n(\mathbb{R})], the set of all [MATH: n \times n] matrices with elements from [MATH: \mathbb{R}]
- [MATH: \mathbb{R}[t]], the set of all polynomials in the variable [MATH: t] and with coefficients from [MATH: \mathbb{R}]
- [MATH: \mathbb{R}_n[t]], the set of all polynomials of degree less than or equal to [MATH: n] in the variable [MATH: t] and with coefficients from [MATH: \mathbb{R}]
- The set of all real-valued functions of one variable.

---

Item 3 — Example: Identifying Sets That Are Not Vector Spaces

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: V] be the set of all real polynomials of degree exactly [MATH: 3], equipped with the usual addition and scalar multiplication operations. Complete the following sentence:

> [MATH: V] is not a vector space because [MATH: \textrm{_________}\,.]

1. the sum of two polynomials of degree [MATH: 3] may not be a polynomial of degree [MATH: 3]
2. [MATH: V] does not contain the polynomial [MATH: -p(x)] for every [MATH: p(x) \in V]
3. addition of polynomials is not commutative

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The correct answer is as follows:

> [MATH: V] is not a vector space because the sum of two polynomials of degree [MATH: 3] may not be a polynomial of degree [MATH: 3].

For instance, if [MATH: p(x) = 1 +x^3] and [MATH: q(x) = 1-x^3], then [MATH: p(x)] and [MATH: q(x)] are in [MATH: V.] However

[MATH: p(x) + q(x)|= (1 + x^{3}) + (1 − x^{3}); = 2 ∉ V.]

On the other hand:

- Addition of polynomials is commutative.
- For any polynomial [MATH: p(x)] of degree [MATH: 3], the corresponding negative polynomial [MATH: -p(x)] also has degree [MATH: 3.]

Item 6 — Example: Proving Statements Using the Vector Space Axioms

Statement:

Proof:

[MATH: w + w|= w|[given]; (w + w) + (− w)|= w + (− w)|[add [math]-\mathbf{w}[/math] to both sides]; w + (w + (− w))|= w + (− w)|[axiom __]; w + 0|= 0|[axiom A4]; w|= 0|[axiom __]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Using the axioms of a vector space, we obtain the following:

[MATH: w + w|= w|[given]; (w + w) + (− w)|= w + (− w)|[add [math]-\mathbf{w}[/math] to both sides]; w + (w + (− w))|= w + (− w)|[axiom [math]{\color{blue}\text{A2}}[/math]]; w + 0|= 0|[axiom A4]; w|= 0|[axiom [math]{\color{blue}\text{A3}}[/math]]]
